chapter: Southwestern bands and New Orleans youth
title: Visiting Buddy in Covington and trumpet feeling
summary: Albert visited Buddy in his shack in Covington to talk music; he admires the feeling of players like Punch Miller.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: So you had a fairly good age even then. That's right. When you went over across the lake into Susquehanna, I think you wrote to Ropeman you went to Mandeville, and then Buddy had a place. In Covington.

To Covington. Right. In Covington. Buddy had an old shack way back in the woods. What would you all talk about? Well, just everything in general. We'd be cooking on his stove and I would share some of his vittles with him, talk about music and at regular procedure, how I'm doing and how you're doing and so forth and so on.
But would he explain to you anything about the trumpet or was it just in general? No, just in general. I didn't know if he gave you any sort of lessons or?
No, I sure wish I could have picked up some of the things he knew. Uh huh.
I wonder if he knew much about chords or if it was all by ear or what?

Well, for what he was playing, he must have known something somehow. Art White was strictly a gift to him because he, well the same with Punch. Punch Miller was a guy that amazed me with what he could do with those three vows. Because his vows were, was one of these real fast-fingering things and there was a lot of, a lot of feeling to it. Not just a lot of notes, there was a lot of feeling coming out of the horn. And here's some of these trumpet players make all of these notes, a thousand notes. And there's no feeling coming, no feeling attached to it. But these guys had a lot of feeling and it was, and the guy that I thought had a tremendous feeling in his horn was Hippolyte Charles. Really?
